newsitem.title: USA: Changes in GDP rate key factor for Fed - sources.
newsitem.headline: Changes in GDP rate key factor for Fed - sources.

text.p: Sharp acceleration or deceleration in the pace of U.S. economic growth, rather than an absolute growth rate, play a key role in shaping U.S. monetary policy, according to sources close to the Federal Reserve.

"The Fed looks at growth on the longer term, like a six-quarter (Gross Domestic Product) average," one source told Reuters, while stressing that single-quarter swings in the GDP growth rate "obviously cannot be interpreted as a change in trend."

The Federal Open Market Committee meets on Tuesday. A majority of analysts in a Reuters survey expect a 25-basis-point hike in the 5.25-percent federal funds rate -- the first such move since February 1, 1995. The Fed last moved on the funds rate -- to lower it by 25 basis points -- on January 31, 1996.

The six-quarter GDP average stood at 3.5 percent at the end of 1994, a year marked by a rapid-fire preemptive tightening cycle that doubled the funds rate. A total of seven hikes shored up the inflation-adjusted real funds rate from zero to clearly restrictive.
By mid-1995, the six-quarter GDP average had dropped to 2.5 percent.

Though the growth rate itself was within the range the Fed regards as consistent with the economy's potential, it had sharply decelerated and was accompanied by an inventory build-up worrisome enough for the Fed to ease in July 1995.

By the end of the second half of 1995, the six-quarter GDP average had fallen to 2.0 percent or the lower end of growth potential estimates. The Fed eased in December 1995 and January 1996 -- the first easing moves at consecutive FOMC meetings since 1992.

The six-quarter GDP average had bounced back to 2.3 percent by mid-1996 and was accompanied by a drop in the jobless rate to 5.5 percent when the Fed introduced a tightening bias at its July meeting last year.
By the end of 1996, the six-quarter GDP average had climbed further to 2.8 percent.

Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan reminded the American public, in three carefully crafted testimonies since late January, that the Fed does not believe economic history can be rewritten or that growth can soar without fueling risks of inflation.
"There is no evidence the business cycle has been repealed," Greenspan told the Senate Banking Committee in his February 26 Humprey-Hawkins.
In past boom-bust cycles, inflation emerged toward the end of an expansion, as consumption slows down and corporations try to maintain profit margins by hiking up prices.

In his testimony before the Joint Economic Committee on March 20, Greenspan pointed out "the importance of acting promptly -- ideally preemptively -- to keep inflation low over the intermediate term and to promote price stability over time."

A second Fed source told Reuters "the need for (monetary) policy to be preemptive is shared, though to different degrees, by everybody at the (19-member) FOMC. The Fed would have to slam harder on the brakes if it waited too long. The cost to the economy would be greater."
Preemptive monetary policy, because it requires the Fed to act before inflationary pressures become embedded in final prices, may be more dificult for the Fed to justify.
Until Greenspan's testimony last Thursday, many Wall Street analysts were still not expecting a tightening because, as one Fed watcher said, "Greenspan lacks a smoking gun."
A number of analysts have ventured the theory that structural changes in the economy may have occurred and resulted in a higher, inflation-free GDP growth rate.
"Regrettably, history is strewn with vision of such 'new eras' that, in the end, have proven to be a mirage," Greenspan remarked in February.
On March 6, Reuters quoted a source close to the Fed saying the odds were the Fed would raise the funds rate by 25 points on March 25.
